chapters.title: Chapter 4: Related Parties and Capital Allocation

lessons.title: Capital Allocation Track Record: Acquisitions, Diversification and Pet Projects

body.text: Over a decade, management's most important job is deciding where the cash goes. Judge them by what that cash earned, not by what they said it would earn.

children.text: Lesson 1 showed that sustainable growth is ROE multiplied by the share of profit retained, and that management's reinvestment choices decide whether that growth actually happens. A company that earns ₹1,000 crore a year and keeps most of it will deploy ₹5,000 crore to ₹10,000 crore over a decade. Where that money goes is the single biggest driver of what the stock is worth ten years from now. Unlike related party leakage, poor capital allocation is usually legal and often well-intentioned. It is still just as expensive.

body.caption: The five uses of cash, and the question to ask about each

cells: New capacity or working capital earns returns above the cost of capital
Is ROCE on the new capital holding up?
The price paid is below the value the acquired business adds
Did the acquired business earn back its price, or was goodwill written off?
The company has a real advantage it can carry into the new field
Why is this company better placed than specialists in that field?
There are no internal opportunities that beat what shareholders can earn elsewhere
The balance sheet needs strengthening, or a clear opportunity is expected
Is idle cash earning anything, and is there a plan for it?

markDefs.definition: The additional operating profit earned on the additional capital a company has deployed over a period. It shows the return on new money, not the average return on all money.

children.text: A company's headline ROCE on screener.in is an average across all the capital it has ever deployed, including old, fully depreciated assets that can flatter the number. To judge recent decisions, use
: how much extra operating profit the company earned for each extra rupee it put to work over five years.

body.caption: Use a five-year window; capital employed = net worth + total debt, or total assets minus current liabilities

children.text: Two illustrative companies both start with ₹5,000 crore of capital employed earning ₹1,000 crore of EBIT, a 20% ROCE. Company X deploys ₹4,000 crore more over five years, into acquisitions and a new unrelated business, and EBIT reaches ₹1,400 crore. Company Y deploys only ₹2,000 crore, into its core business, and EBIT reaches ₹1,500 crore.

stats.label: Company X incremental ROCE
stats.context: ₹400 crore extra EBIT on ₹4,000 crore extra capital

stats.label: Company Y incremental ROCE

stats.label: The trap
stats.context: Bigger, but every new rupee earned half the old return

children.text: Company X's management can truthfully say revenue, assets, and EBIT all grew. Its ROCE of 15.6% still looks respectable. But its new capital earned just 10% before tax, likely below its cost of capital, so the expansion destroyed value. Company Y used half the capital and produced more profit. This is why a falling ROCE trend on screener.in during a heavy investment phase deserves a closer look.

body.title: Calculate Incremental ROCE
body.prompt: Over five years, a company's capital employed rose from ₹6,000 crore to ₹8,500 crore, and its EBIT rose from ₹900 crore to ₹1,150 crore. What was its incremental ROCE?
body.explanation: Extra EBIT = ₹1,150 - ₹900 = ₹250 crore. Extra capital = ₹8,500 - ₹6,000 = ₹2,500 crore. Incremental ROCE = ₹250 ÷ ₹2,500 = 10%, against a starting ROCE of 15%. The company's recent investments are earning less than its existing business, dragging its overall returns down.

children.text: Measure 2: Value Created per Rupee Retained

A simple long-term test: every rupee of profit a company keeps instead of paying out should, over time, turn into at least a rupee of market value. If it does not, shareholders would have been better off receiving it as a dividend.

body.latex: \text{Value Created per Rupee Retained} = \frac{\text{Market Cap}_{\text{end}} - \text{Market Cap}_{\text{start}}}{\text{Cumulative Retained Earnings over the Period}}
body.caption: Use a 10-year window to smooth out market moods; adjust for any fresh equity raised
Two companies, each retained ₹6,000 crore over 10 years (₹ crore)

cells: Shareholders would have been better off with dividends

body.text: You can get cumulative retained earnings quickly from screener.in: add up net profit minus dividends paid over the period, or simply compare the growth in reserves. Remember to deduct any QIPs or rights issues from the market cap increase, since value bought with new shareholder money is not value created from retained profit.

children.text: Acquisitions: Reading the Deal and the Aftermath

body.title: Acquisitions That Tend to Work vs Those That Tend Not To

columns.label: Tend to Work
points: Small relative to the acquirer, often bolt-ons in the same category
Clear fit with existing distribution, customers, or manufacturing
Reasonable price, funded mainly from internal cash
A history of similar deals the company has integrated successfully
Specific, measurable targets disclosed at announcement

columns.label: Tend to Destroy Value
points: Very large relative to the acquirer, described as 'transformational'
Overseas trophy assets bought near the top of a cycle
Target owned by the promoter group
Vague synergy claims with no disclosed targets or timelines

children.text: The best after-the-fact scorecard for acquisitions is in the notes to accounts: goodwill and its impairment. When a company pays more than the fair value of the net assets it buys, the excess is recorded as goodwill. When the business fails to deliver, the company must write goodwill down. An impairment is management's formal admission, years later, that it overpaid.

events.title: Tata Steel wins Corus
events.description: After a bidding contest, Tata Steel agrees to buy Anglo-Dutch steelmaker Corus for about US$12 billion, making it one of the largest overseas acquisitions by an Indian company. It is financed largely with debt, close to the peak of the global steel cycle.

events.title: The cycle turns
events.description: The global financial crisis and weak European steel demand hit the acquired business. Tata Steel records large impairments on its European assets over the following years.

events.title: Plan to sell the UK business
events.description: Facing continued losses, Tata Steel announces it will explore selling its UK operations.

events.title: European JV blocked
events.description: A planned joint venture combining Tata Steel's European business with thyssenkrupp's is blocked by the European Commission, leaving Tata Steel to restructure the business on its own.

children.text: Corus was not a governance failure in the sense of fraud or leakage. It was a very large, debt-funded, overseas acquisition at the top of a cycle, the exact profile in the right-hand column above. It shows that capital allocation risk exists even in groups with strong governance reputations, and that its cost can take more than a decade to fully play out.

The most dangerous capital allocation decisions in Indian markets are often not acquisitions but diversifications driven by the promoter's ambitions: an airline, a sports venture, real estate, or a string of new industries far from the company's strengths. They tend to share one pattern. A profitable core business generates the cash, and a promoter's pet project consumes it.

cells: Kingfisher Airlines, launched in 2005, which later bought Air Deccan
The airline piled up losses and debt, and was grounded in October 2012
Expressways, large real estate projects, and the Buddh International Circuit, which hosted Formula One from 2011 to 2013
Heavy debt led to asset sales, and group company Jaypee Infratech entered insolvency in 2017
Large overseas acquisitions including Germany's REpower in 2007, largely debt funded
Defaulted on foreign currency convertible bonds in 2012 and went through debt restructuring
The pledge spiral covered in Lesson 7

body.text: Pet projects rarely appear as a single dramatic announcement. They grow through small, repeated investments: an equity infusion into a new subsidiary one year, a loan the next, a corporate guarantee after that. Track the cumulative amount the listed company has put into any non-core business, and compare it with what that business has ever earned.

body.title: Spot the Weakest Capital Allocator
body.question: Over the last ten years, which management team shows the weakest capital allocation?
options: A paints company that made several small acquisitions in adjacent categories, all profitable, with ROCE stable above 25%
A cement company that tripled capacity, funded mainly from internal cash, with ROCE steady at about 18%

An auto components maker that entered real estate, hospitality, and a sports franchise, with the listed company investing ₹2,400 crore in total, ROCE falling from 22% to 11%, and ₹900 crore of goodwill and investments written off
An FMCG company that could not find good reinvestment opportunities and paid out 90% of profits as dividends
body.explanation: Option C shows every sign of pet-project diversification: unrelated businesses, large cumulative investment, collapsing ROCE, and write-offs that admit the money was lost. Options A and B redeployed capital into related businesses at high returns. Option D is not a bad allocator; returning cash that cannot be reinvested well is a sound decision.

body.title: The Transformational Acquisition
body.scenario: An NSE-listed mid cap pharma company with a market cap of ₹8,000 crore, net cash on its balance sheet, and a 10-year ROCE averaging 24% announces it will acquire a US generic drug maker for US$1.2 billion, about ₹10,000 crore. The deal will be funded with ₹7,500 crore of new debt and ₹2,500 crore from a QIP. The target has been loss-making for two years because of US price erosion. Management calls it 'transformational' and says it will 'unlock significant synergies', but gives no numbers. The promoter family has no connection to the target. The company's two previous overseas acquisitions, both much smaller, were written down within five years.
body.prompt: How would you evaluate this decision, and what would you need to see to support it?
body.modelAnswer: This deal has most of the characteristics of value-destroying acquisitions. It is larger than the acquirer's entire market cap, turns a net cash company into a heavily indebted one, and dilutes existing shareholders through a QIP. The target is loss-making in a market with known price erosion. Synergies are claimed but not quantified. And management's own track record on smaller overseas deals is two write-downs. There is no related party issue here, so it is not a leakage problem, but it is a serious capital allocation risk that could permanently lower the company's ROCE from its 24% history. To support it, you would need disclosed synergy targets and timelines, a clear explanation of why the target's losses are temporary, the price paid relative to the target's revenue and asset value, a credible plan and timeline to reduce the new debt, and an explanation of what went wrong in the previous acquisitions and what has changed. Without these, the reasonable response is to reduce exposure and track incremental ROCE and goodwill impairment over the next three years.

body.title: Build a 10-Year Capital Allocation Scorecard
steps: On screener.in, note capital employed and EBIT at the start and end of the last five and ten years, and calculate incremental ROCE for each window
Plot the ROCE trend for ten years and mark any years of heavy capex, acquisitions, or new business launches
Calculate cumulative retained earnings over ten years and value created per rupee retained, adjusting for any fresh equity raised
From the annual reports, list every acquisition and new business entered: year, amount invested, and funding source
Check the goodwill and investments notes for impairments or write-offs linked to those deals
Add up total money put into non-core subsidiaries through equity, loans, and guarantees, and compare with their cumulative profit or loss in Form AOC-1
Rate management: did capital go where returns were highest, or where the promoter's ambitions pointed?

body.text: Companies named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures and widely reported events, for education only. The numerical examples are illustrative. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Capital allocation over a decade is management's biggest influence on shareholder value, and poor allocation is expensive even when it is legal
Incremental ROCE, extra EBIT divided by extra capital employed, shows what new investment is earning; in the illustration, Company X's new capital earned 10% while Company Y's earned 25%
Value created per rupee retained tests whether keeping profit beat paying it out: ₹2.00 is good allocation, ₹0.50 is not
Large, debt-funded, overseas or 'transformational' acquisitions carry the highest risk; goodwill impairments are management's later admission of overpaying
Tata Steel's Corus deal shows capital allocation risk even in well-governed groups; Kingfisher Airlines, Jaypee, and Suzlon show the cost of ambition-led diversification
Pet projects grow through repeated small infusions, loans, and guarantees, so track cumulative investment in non-core businesses against what they have earned
